name: GNOME Web
summary: Web browser for the GNOME desktop, built on the WebKit engine and delivered as Epiphany, with a deliberately minimal interface and built-in tracking prevention.
license: GNU General Public License, version 3 (repository COPYING file)

content.introduction:
GNOME Web is the web browser of the GNOME desktop. It is published under the code name Epiphany, and both names refer to the same application: the GNOME app page states that Web is often referred to by its code name, Epiphany, while the project's own README is titled GNOME Web and explains the codename by a dictionary definition — "a usually sudden manifestation or perception of the essential nature or meaning of something".

The version landmark used here is the one published on the official application page: latest version 51.1, released on 24 September 2026. That release sits in the GNOME 51 cycle, whose release notes are dated 16 September 2026.

The browser is written for Linux systems and is distributed primarily as a Flatpak from Flathub. Its declared principles are simplicity, standards compliance and software freedom, and it is explicitly designed for non-technical users rather than for web developers.
content.origin_and_history:
The documentation read does not publish a creation date for the project, and this entry does not supply one. What the sources date is the release being described and the improvements that came with each GNOME cycle.

The project presents itself through a manifesto rather than a chronology. Its README sets out three principles and argues each one: simplicity, because "feature bloat and user interface clutter is evil" and because the browser should do one thing well, in the spirit of the UNIX philosophy; standards compliance, because the success of non-standard features can lead one browser to dominate the market and reduce the freedom of choice; and software freedom, because the source code is published under a licence that respects freedom. The same text names Google Chrome as an example of a browser that "purports to be open source, yet actually includes several proprietary components", and presents Epiphany as fully free software.

The documented history that can be dated is recent and comes from the GNOME release notes. In GNOME 49, published on 17 September 2025, Web received "a major round of improvements and bug fixes", with more than a hundred issues resolved, together with a site-specific menu in the address entry, optional regional ad block lists, an estimated reading time in reader mode, improved smartcard support, a dedicated password management dialog, a redesigned security dialog, controls to quit or uninstall a web app from its menu, OpenSearch integration with live search suggestions, case-sensitive and whole-word in-page search, and a new bookmark editing mode. In GNOME 51, published on 16 September 2026, the release notes describe a keyboard shortcut to copy the current page address, secure password generation through the `pwquality` library, another round of password manager fixes, and an address bar where search engine suggestions no longer show their URLs.

Two maintainers are listed on the application page: Jan-Michael Brummer and Michael Catanzaro.
content.rendering_engine_and_technical_architect:
GNOME Web renders pages with WebKit. The project README states that Epiphany is "a GNOME web browser based on the WebKit rendering engine", and the WebKitGTK project describes WebKitGTK as "a full-featured port of the WebKit rendering engine" that is "the official web engine of the GNOME platform" and is used in browsers such as Epiphany, alongside Wike and Web Apps.

WebKitGTK documents the architectural points that matter for a browser built on it. Since support for WebKit2 was added, applications can use the web platform with the web content placed in a separate process, so that a page cannot crash the main application or freeze its user interface. Audio and video are handled through the GStreamer backend. Rendering can use the GPU for page compositing, scrolling, 3D CSS transforms and WebGL. Accessibility is described as a core value of the port.

The build documentation adds a practical consequence: Epiphany itself is a comparatively small application that depends on WebKit, and changing behaviour inside the engine means rebuilding WebKit. The README recommends Toolbox or JHBuild for that case and gives the commands to build WebKitGTK from the WebKit repository. Development versions of Epiphany are distributed as Flatpak bundles that bundle newer WebKitGTK builds, which is how the project lets testers exercise engine changes before they reach distributions.

Four layers are worth distinguishing: WebKit is the engine, WebKitGTK the Linux and GNOME port of that engine, Epiphany the browser built on it, and the GNOME release cycle the schedule that bundles the two together twice a year. A behaviour described in WebKitGTK documentation therefore applies to GNOME Web only through that port.
content.interface_and_documented_features:
The interface is deliberately reduced. The project states that it aims to present "the simplest interface possible for a browser", that it follows the GNOME Human Interface Guidelines unless there are serious reasons not to, and that it is cautious about adding preferences because preferences come with a cost.

The user help documents the features that exist: browsing and tab handling, browsing history recalled while typing in the address bar, password storage and removal, certificate management, deletion of cookies and of personal data stored by websites, a per-site preference for data storage, proxy configuration, private browsing, local file viewing, downloading files with a configurable destination, a custom font for pages, custom CSS to override page themes, mouse gestures, creation and removal of web apps, and restoration of a closed tab.

Web apps are a distinctive feature: a site can be installed so that it opens in its own window, and from the GNOME 49 cycle it can also be quit or uninstalled directly from its menu. The GNOME 49 notes add a site menu in the address entry for actions relating to the open website, an estimated reading time in reader mode, and OpenSearch integration: when a visited site supports OpenSearch, a button appears in the address entry to add it as a search engine, with live suggestions. The GNOME 51 notes add `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `C` to copy the address of the current page without opening the address bar, and generation of strong passwords through `pwquality`.

No page read documents an extension catalogue of its own. The project's stated ambition is a browser for web users, not for web developers, and the few developer-oriented tools it accepts, such as the web inspector, are described as welcome only if unobtrusive.
content.installation_and_distribution:
The recommended installation route is Flatpak from Flathub. The README calls Flatpak "the best application distribution mechanism for Linux" and warns that packages provided by operating system package managers "are often outdated and insecure", while acknowledging that they usually exist.

Three Flatpak flavours are documented. The stable version comes from Flathub, whose page for the application lists a 14 MiB download, the x86_64 and aarch64 architectures and a low-risk safety rating. Epiphany Technology Preview is published from the nightly GNOME repository and is described as "not stable". Epiphany Canary, installed with a single `flatpak --user install` command against the nightly repository, builds directly from WebKit's main branch and Epiphany's master branch and is described as "very unstable".

Building from source is documented twice: the recommended route is the flatpak-builder manifest opened in GNOME Builder, which provides all dependencies; the manual route uses Meson and Ninja, with the caveat that several pkg-config dependencies must be installed first, and the README gives the commands for RPM-based and deb-based distributions. Rebuilding WebKit itself requires Toolbox or JHBuild.

The release history visible on Flathub also shows that packaging carries security work: one recent stable update lists, among the fixed bugs, an entry referenced as CVE-2026-94291 concerning an insecure iframe reachable through the view-source and `ephy-reader` schemes.
content.platforms_and_hardware_architectures:
GNOME Web is designed for Linux systems; the README says so in one sentence ("Epiphany is designed for Linux systems") and the project states that its main goal is integration with GNOME and with similar desktops, notably elementary OS, adding that it does not aim to make the browser usable outside those environments. No Windows or macOS build is documented in the sources read for this entry, and the application page lists Linux among its keywords.

On the hardware side, the Flathub page publishes two architectures, x86_64 and aarch64, which is the only explicit statement about processor support found in the sources. Minimum system versions are not published by the project: they are set by the Flatpak runtime and, for distribution packages, by each distribution.

This absence is a documentary fact rather than an omission. A browser distributed mainly as a Flatpak inherits the platform requirements of its runtime, which the project does not restate; the application page simply points to Flathub for installation.
content.extensions_and_add_on_store:
No extension store is documented for GNOME Web in the sources read, and this entry does not claim one exists. What the documentation describes instead is a small set of built-in extensions to the browsing experience rather than a third-party catalogue.

The most documented of those mechanisms is content blocking. The README states that GNOME Web regularly downloads updated ad block filter lists from the `ublock-webkit-filters` GitHub project, and that users who are concerned about the browser connecting automatically to GitHub can disable this feature in the preferences. The GNOME 49 release notes describe better ad blocking, with support for optional regional ad block lists.

Tracking prevention is likewise built in rather than added: the README states that GNOME Web enables Intelligent Tracking Prevention by default, that it includes many other tracking prevention measures, and that WebKit's tracking prevention documentation should be consulted for details. WebKit itself provides the filter-list and content-blocking mechanisms, so the feature set follows the engine rather than a store.

For anyone coming from browsers with an extension marketplace, the practical consequence is stated plainly: features are either built into the browser or provided by the engine, and there is no documented marketplace in which to install an add-on. That absence is documented here as a fact of scope, not as a temporary gap.
content.privacy_and_security_model:
Privacy is presented as built in. The application page summarises the browser as one "with built-in privacy", and the README documents the two mechanisms that carry that claim: Intelligent Tracking Prevention enabled by default, with other measures delegated to WebKit's tracking prevention documentation, and filter lists refreshed from a public GitHub project, which can be turned off.

Data handling is described in a privacy statement that the project reproduces in its README because Mozilla's terms of service require it. By default the browser stores personal data such as bookmarks and browsing history locally on the computer, for the user's own use; that data is never transmitted to the GNOME Web developers and never to a third party unless the user chooses to enable the optional Sync integration, in which case data is encrypted and transmitted to Mozilla's Firefox Sync server and stored there in encrypted form. The statement adds that GNOME Web uses the Firefox Sync service but is not Firefox and is not produced or endorsed by Mozilla.

Security features documented in the GNOME 49 cycle are smartcard support, a dedicated password management dialog and a redesigned security dialog; the GNOME 51 cycle adds generation of strong passwords through `pwquality`. The help pages cover certificate management and the deletion of cookies and site data. A published security fix, referenced as CVE-2026-94291 in the Flathub release notes, concerned an insecure iframe reachable through the view-source and `ephy-reader` schemes.

Three reservations belong here. Enabling Sync moves data to a third-party service, even if encrypted, and is therefore a choice rather than a default. Ad block lists are fetched from a public code hosting service, an outbound connection that the project itself describes and lets users disable. And privacy, security and anonymity remain distinct questions: the documented features reduce tracking, they do not make the browser an anonymity tool, and the project does not claim that it is one.
content.update_channels_and_release_cadence:
Three channels are documented, and they differ in stability rather than in intended audience. The stable channel is the Flathub build, currently version 51.1 released on 24 September 2026. Epiphany Technology Preview follows the project's development branch and is described as not stable. Epiphany Canary is built from WebKit's main branch and Epiphany's master branch together, is installed by a single command, and is described as very unstable.

The cadence is that of GNOME. The GNOME 49 notes are dated 17 September 2025 and the GNOME 51 notes 16 September 2026, which documents a six-monthly cycle, and the browser's version number tracks it. Between two cycles, point releases such as 51.1 carry fixes and translations, and the Flatpak metadata shows those fixes, including security fixes, reaching users through the stable channel rather than through a separate advisory list only.

The repository README does not describe an automatic update mechanism of its own; updates arrive with the distribution channel used — the Flatpak remote for the recommended installation, the distribution's packages otherwise. Anyone installing from source, or using one of the two testing channels, is outside the stable cadence by construction.
content.licensing_and_governance:
The code is published under the GNU General Public License, version 3: the repository's COPYING file contains the version 3 text of that licence, dated 29 June 2007. The manifesto in the README treats that choice as substantive rather than incidental, presenting software freedom as one of the project's three principles and arguing that the licence must respect the user's freedom.

Governance is that of a GNOME project. Development happens on the GNOME GitLab instance, where the source, the issue tracker and the merge requests live; the application page points to the issue tracker, to the GNOME welcome page for contributors, to the translation platform `l10n.gnome.org`, to a Matrix room for the community, and to donations to the GNOME Foundation. Contact for discussion is a Discourse forum tag rather than a mailing list. Two maintainers are named on the application page.

Two consequences follow for readers. First, the browser is free software end to end, in contrast with browsers that publish part of their code while shipping proprietary components, a distinction the project makes explicitly. Second, the project's direction is set inside GNOME's release process, so the browser follows the desktop's design language and cycle rather than a standalone product roadmap — which is also why its version numbers match GNOME's.
content.limitations_and_scope:
The scope is narrow by design and should be read as such. The browser targets Linux desktop environments close to GNOME; the project says it does not aim to make it usable outside GNOME and similar desktops. No Windows, macOS or Android build is documented in the sources read. Features are deliberately limited: the project states that preferences are added cautiously and that interface clutter is treated as a defect, and the help pages list a feature set narrower than that of mainstream browsers.

No extension catalogue is documented, so capabilities come from the browser and the engine rather than from add-ons. Some behaviour depends on services the project does not operate: Sync relies on Mozilla's Firefox Sync servers, and filter lists are downloaded from a public GitHub project, both of which can be a problem in constrained or monitored networks, and the filter list download can be disabled.

Three documentary limits apply to this entry. The sources read publish no creation date, so no founding date is given here. They publish no minimum hardware configuration beyond the two Flatpak architectures. And they do not describe a complete feature-by-feature comparison with other browsers; the GNOME release notes describe what changed in a cycle, not what has been dropped, so an absence in this entry should not be read as proof that a feature does not exist.
content.who_is_it_for: GNOME Web is intended for people who use a GNOME or GNOME-like desktop and want a simple browser that follows the system's interface conventions, installs as a Flatpak, blocks tracking by default and does not ask to be configured. The project states that it targets non-technical users by design. It also suits users who care that the browser is free software end to end and who prefer web apps and a small fixed feature set to a large extension ecosystem.
content.who_is_it_not_for: It is not aimed at Windows or macOS users, since no build for those systems is documented, nor at users outside GNOME-style desktops, which the project explicitly excludes from its goals. It is not a browser for people who rely on a large third-party extension catalogue, nor for those who need fine-grained preferences, given the project's stated caution about adding them. It is not an anonymity tool: its documented privacy features reduce tracking, while optional Sync depends on Mozilla's servers.
content.verdict: GNOME Web is a small, opinionated browser with a clear position: a WebKitGTK engine, a deliberately minimal interface, tracking prevention enabled by default, GPLv3 licensing and Linux-only distribution through Flatpak. What the documentation establishes is precise — version 51.1 released on 24 September 2026, the engine and its separate web process, the Flatpak channel structure with two testing builds, the privacy statement around local storage and optional Firefox Sync, and the per-cycle feature additions recorded by GNOME's release notes. What it also establishes, by omission, is a scope: no extension marketplace, no Windows or macOS target, no published minimum configuration. That narrowness is the product's design, not a gap in its documentation, and it is what makes the entry legible next to browsers that choose the opposite trade-off.
